div.p: When I revolve in my mind and call up the memory of Octavius, my good and most faithful companion, so great a sweetness and affection for the man clings to me that I seem in some sort to return into the past myself, rather than merely to recall by remembrance things now done and gone:

For on business and for the sake of visiting me he had hurried to Rome, leaving his home, his wife, his children, and—what is most lovable in children—those still of innocent years, attempting words yet but half-formed, a speech the sweeter for the very stumbling and breaking of the tongue.

Then Octavius said: "It is not the part of a good man, brother Marcus, thus to abandon in this blindness of vulgar ignorance one who clings to your side at home and abroad, so that on so bright a day you suffer him to stumble upon stones, fashioned indeed and anointed and crowned, when you know that the disgrace of this error redounds no less to you than to himself."

So, while we were all taken with the pleasure of this spectacle, Caecilius gave no heed and did not laugh at the contest, but, silent, anxious, and apart, by his face confessed some grief I could not tell.

Then Caecilius began thus: "Although to you, brother Marcus, there is no doubt about that very thing we are now chiefly inquiring into, since, having carefully tried both ways of living, you have rejected the one and approved the other, yet for the present your mind must be so framed that you hold the balance of a most impartial judge, and do not lean weighted toward one side, lest your verdict seem to be born not so much from our discussions as brought forth from your own feelings.

Since, therefore, fortune is fixed or nature uncertain, how much more reverent and better it is to receive, as a high priest of truth, the teaching of our forefathers, to cultivate the religions handed down, to adore the gods whom from our parents we were imbued to fear before we knew them familiarly, and not to pass judgement upon the divinities, but to trust our predecessors, who in an age still rude, at the very birth of the world, deserved to have the gods either gracious or for kings! Hence indeed throughout all empires, provinces, and towns we see that peoples have their own several rites of worship and honour their local gods: as the Eleusinians Ceres, the Phrygians the Mother, the Epidaurians Aesculapius, the Chaldaeans Belus, the Syrians Astarte, the Taurians Diana, the Gauls Mercury, the Romans all of these.

Yet not rashly—for I venture meanwhile even myself to concede this, and so to err the more safely—did our forefathers devote their pains to observing auguries, consulting entrails, instituting sacred rites, and dedicating temples.

And so, since among all nations, however uncertain be the reason or the origin of it, there yet remains a firm agreement concerning the immortal gods, I cannot endure anyone, swollen with such audacity and such irreligious—I know not what—wisdom, who strives to dissolve or weaken this religion, so ancient, so useful, so wholesome.

And now, as worse things spring up the more fruitfully, with corrupt morals creeping on from day to day, throughout the whole world these foulest sanctuaries of an impious gathering grow up. This conspiracy must be utterly rooted out and abhorred.
Many things I purposely pass over: for these too are far too many, all or most of which are declared to be true by the very obscurity of this depraved religion.

What of this, that they threaten conflagration to the whole world and to the very universe with its stars, and contrive its ruin, as if either the eternal order established by the divine laws of nature could be disturbed, or, the bond of all the elements being broken and the heavenly framework sundered, this mass by which it is contained and girt could be overthrown?
Nor do you take even from the present any proof how the empty vows of an idle promise deceive you: while you yet live, estimate, you wretches, what hangs over you after death.

And yet, if you have a passion for philosophising, let whoever of you is great enough imitate, if he can, Socrates, the prince of wisdom. Famous is the answer of that man, as often as he was asked about heavenly things: 'What is above us is nothing to us.'
